#WATCH | Thiruvananthapuram: On LPG issue, Kerala Minister for Food and Civil Supplies, G. R. Anil says, “As someone who personally heard the statement made by the Union Petroleum Minister in Parliament, I must say that it has no connection with the ground reality. I do not know how severe the situation is in other parts of the country, but in Kerala the shortage of LPG cylinders has become extremely serious. Kerala is largely a consumer state, and the present crisis has started affecting the daily lives of people across the state. While it is being claimed that domestic consumers will receive cylinders as required, the reality is that many families are approaching us with complaints about non-availability. Another major issue is that people who depend on private gas agencies are facing great difficulty in getting cylinders. Even though public sector oil companies claim that they are supplying without fail, those who rely on private agencies are struggling to receive their supply. At the same time, consumers are also facing serious difficulties in booking cylinders from public sector oil companies. When I spoke to the companies, they said the initial problems were due to capacity limitations and technical issues, and that they had installed a new server to resolve them. However, despite these assurances, the problems are still continuing. The situation is even more serious for non-domestic consumers. Many hotels and small establishments are on the verge of closing down because they are unable to get cylinders. Even places with heavy public footfall are being supplied only on a priority basis, and that too is not enough to meet the demand. The Union Petroleum Minister, Suresh Gopi, must open his eyes and see the real situation in Kerala. Being a Malayali, he knows the conditions in the state very well and should understand the gravity of the issue. Only if the present limitations in the supply of cylinders are addressed and the allocation to Kerala is increased can this crisis be resolved. In a meeting convened by the Chief Minister to review the situation, when we discussed the matter with the companies, they informed us that they currently have the capacity and stock to supply only about 20 percent of the demand from non-domestic consumers. Even if we reorganise the distribution, only a limited section can be served, while a large number of consumers will still remain without supply. Therefore, increasing the allocation of LPG cylinders to Kerala is the only real solution. The Union Petroleum Minister and the ministry must understand the facts and take immediate steps. Statements made merely based on collected information, without understanding the ground reality, have no relevance. When this issue emerged, the Kerala government immediately took steps. We sent a letter to the Union Minister and called meetings with the companies operating in the state to review the situation. Arrangements were made to monitor stock positions daily through district collectors and hold discussions at regular intervals to reduce the severity of the crisis. We also examined whether additional kerosene could be supplied in areas where it is possible, to support ordinary people. This issue will not affect only cooking fuel; it will have a wider impact. Even laboratories where patients go for medical tests could face difficulties, and the functioning of crematoriums may also be affected. Small roadside eateries and many other establishments depend on LPG. If this situation continues, it will lead to a serious crisis across sectors and may trigger widespread price increases. I repeat, the situation is very serious. The Centre must recognise this and act immediately. Since the Union Minister is a Malayali who understands Kerala well, I am raising this issue by directly referring to him and urging urgent intervention.” (14.03.2026)

We are pleased to welcome back Dr. Deepak Mishra as a Distinguished Professor (Visiting) at ICRIER. Dr. Mishra currently serves as Adviser to the World Development Report 2026 on AI for Development and previously led ICRIER as its Director and Chief Executive from 2021 to 2025. Dr. Mishra’s research area lies at the intersection of technology and development, with a particular focus on digital transformation, jobs, growth and globalization. With more than two decades of experience at the World Bank, he has worked across Africa, South Asia, and East Asia, and co-directed the World Development Report 2016: Digital Dividends. Dr. Mishra holds an M.A. in Economics from the Delhi School of Economics and a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Maryland. To learn more about his work, please visit: mishradeepak.com We look forward to benefiting from his insights and leadership in advancing research and policy dialogue at ICRIER.

Estas organizaciones de “defensa de los derechos humanos”, a las que muchos medios nacionales e internacionales (The Guardian, France 24, El País, los medios de Open Society, entre otros) les están dando amplia cobertura, y que están siendo retomados por miles de periodistas, activistas y políticos locales y extranjeros, están exigiendo que el Estado de El Salvador libere al 100% de los pandilleros capturados desde el inicio del Régimen de Excepción. Ya ni siquiera lo disimulan. Literalmente afirman que “más de 89,000 personas fueron capturadas arbitrariamente”, que sus derechos humanos están siendo violados y que se han cometido crímenes de lesa humanidad. Bajo esa lógica, la liberación del 100% de los detenidos pasaría a ser una obligación de todo Estado. Incluso, en su exposición, uno de los “expertos” deja claro que su denuncia no se refiere únicamente a supuestos opositores políticos o a personas inocentes, sino que también incluye a “miembros de pandillas o personas percibidas como tales”, sosteniendo que, en todos los casos (los 89,000), se trata de capturas arbitrarias, constitutivas de crímenes de lesa humanidad y violaciones a los derechos humanos. Me alegra que se hayan quitado la máscara, porque antes siempre intentaban matizar sus denuncias. Ahora lo han dicho con claridad: Quieren la liberación del 100% de los pandilleros y que El Salvador vuelva al estado en que se encontraba antes del Régimen de Excepción; es decir, al país más peligroso del mundo. Observen quiénes retoman este supuesto estudio y quiénes lo validan como verdadero. Ellos quieren que los criminales sigan asesinando inocentes; para eso trabajan, para eso les pagan. Su labor es engañar a la población para debilitar el apoyo a medidas que pueden traer seguridad a sus familias. Su verdadero objetivo es perpetuar el sufrimiento de la gente honrada. Las organizaciones de derechos humanos se han convertido en los bufetes legales de los delincuentes. ICRIER in collaboration with @Bruegel_org, hosted a panel discussion on “The Mother of All Deals? Economic Implications of the India-EU FTA” The discussion brought together leading experts Pritam Banerjee, Head, @CWS_iift; @ignaciobercero, Senior Fellow, Bruegel; @profarpita1, Professor, #ICRIER; and André Sapir, Senior Fellow, Bruegel to examine the potential economic and strategic implications of the India–EU Free Trade Agreement for both sides, as well as its impact on the global trading system. The session was moderated by @ShekharAiyar, Director & Chief Executive, ICRIER, and the keynote address was delivered by @WeyandSabine, Director-General, DG @Trade_EU @EU_Commission. The session explored several key questions, including: 🔹 What are the main benefits for India from this deal—including for labor-intensive sectors like apparel and footwear—and how will these contribute to the aim to become #ViksitBharat2047? 🔹 What are the main benefits for the EU from this deal? Which sectors and industries are expected to gain the most: is it advanced tech, capital goods, agricultural goods, services? 🔹 What are some of the misses from Indian perspective in this agreement? With India signing several FTAs, why is this the “Mother of all Deals”? How does it compare it with other FTAs like the India-UK FTA? 🔹 Is the deal WTO compatible? What are its implications for the rules-based multilateral trading system? ▶️ To learn more about the discussion, watch the full recording on our YouTube channel : youtube.com/watch?v=ChoqjY33… #IndiaEUFTA #TradePolicy #PolicyDiscussion #ExpertDialogue #TradeAndEconomics

Did you know 😏 He rubbed lemon juice on his face. Robbed two banks. Smiled at the cameras. Got caught in an hour. And changed psychology forever. In 1995, McArthur Wheeler walked into two banks in Pittsburgh and robbed them with no mask, no disguise, and lemon juice on his face. He believed that because lemon juice works as invisible ink on paper, it would make his face invisible to cameras. He smiled directly into the security cameras. Police aired the footage on the evening news and arrested him within an hour. When shown the tape, Wheeler stared at the screen and said, "But I wore the juice." He had tested the theory with a Polaroid selfie and didn't appear in the photo — because lemon juice got in his eyes and he aimed the camera at the ceiling. His case inspired Cornell psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger to publish their 1999 paper defining the Dunning-Kruger Effect — the cognitive bias where people with low ability drastically overestimate their own competence.

The recruitment rally witnessed enthusiastic participation from local youth from villages located near the Line of Control. The initiative is aimed at strengthening operational logistics support for troops deployed in difficult mountainous terrain while simultaneously providing employment opportunities to the local population. Defence porters play a vital role in supporting soldiers deployed in high-altitude and forward operational areas by assisting in the transportation of supplies, equipment, rations, and essential materials to remote posts that are often inaccessible by vehicles. Their contribution becomes especially crucial in challenging terrains like the Krishna Ghati sector, where steep mountains, dense forests, and extreme weather conditions make logistics operations highly demanding. The Indian Army has consistently engaged with border communities through such initiatives, ensuring that local youth become partners in national security while also benefiting from employment opportunities and skill development. Another thread on Iran. The attack (or the “excursion”) on Iran, after the forceful removal of Venezuela’s President Nicolas Maduro, may have brought US foreign policy to an all-time low – both in terms of how the world views US power and for how damaging American foreign action will be to the domestic economy. This isn’t, of course, the first time the US has undertaken an ill-fated, poorly-planned intervention abroad. Arguably, an important one was CIA’s toppling of Iran’s popularly-elected prime minister Mohammad Mossadegh in 1953, after he nationalized the British-owned oil industry of Iran with the strong support of Iran’s parliament. History is contingent, and it would be a stretch to say that Mossadegh’s ouster necessarily caused the Iranian revolution and its aftermath. But there should be little doubt that CIA’s brazen intervention shaped the way that many Iranians viewed the regime of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, instituted (or “restored”) as Shah by the Americans, as a puppet of an imperialist power. This was the reason why many segments of Iranian population, including communists, conservatives and liberals, supported the Iranian revolution of Ayatollah Khomeini against Pahlavi. Khomeini was, in hindsight, anything but a consensus leader, quickly turning violently against his erstwhile allies and setting up a hugely repressive, theocratic regime, which is still in power in Iran. The general lesson for today should be that US interventions will have plenty of unforeseen consequences, in part because they will inevitably create resentment. Most people around the world don’t like the power from the outside coming in and acting like a bully. This is all the more so when the outside intervention doesn’t have a coherent ideological justification – during the Cold War, the United States had the overarching objective of stopping the spread of communism (which was a real threat). It is even more so when the action is ill-planned, shows no understanding or concern for the lives of the people it is affecting, and is arrogant. We may now expect US soft power around the globe to reach an all-time low (except that the Trump administration doesn’t seem to care about soft power). True, the Iranian regime under Ayatollah Khamenei (Khomeini’s successor as the supreme leader) was singularly vicious and repressive. The majority of the population holds no love for either Khamenei or the Revolutionary Guard. But this doesn’t mean the regime will collapse. Nor does it imply that the intervention will bring peace and stability to the region. The most remarkable thing about the Israeli-American attack on Iran is how poorly planned it was – even compared to CIA actions during the Cold War that sometimes had disastrous outcomes. I don’t mean that the American Israeli military did not have well-scoped targets and precision bombs, which they did (for the most part). Rather, they did not have a clear (or any) exit plan. It should have been obvious that the Iranian regime wouldn’t collapse, even if its head were cut off. It should have also been viewed as probable that Iran would retaliate in a way that would bring instability to the region and higher oil prices. After all, the Iranian regime’s strongest trump card is to block the Strait of Hormuz, which would hike global oil prices. In fact, many in the Iranian elite may think that they have a fairly solid hand. Americans wouldn’t have an appetite for a prolonged war, while the Iranian regime can continue with the blockade for a long time and still suppress the population to ensure its survival. All the current market consternation seems to confirm this. The consequence is higher oil prices and uncertainty in the global economy. At a time when the economy seems fragile (as witnessed by the frequent discussions of an AI bubble), this is a recipe for trouble. Higher oil prices will slow down investment and economic growth, and push up prices. The resulting higher unemployment and inflation are bound to be costly for any government (including those in Europe who are being threatened by right-wing populist outsiders, despite the fact that most European leaders are opposing the war). In the United States, this will be seen as Trump’s war (or a Trump-Israeli war). So he should pay the political price for it. But here is the catch. Trump himself is the anti-establishment leader. If a segment of the US electorate blames not Trump primarily but the political establishment for the ensuing economic problems, this can further polarize the country and weaken US institutions. Trump himself is likely to throw oil on this fire (if a pun could be forgiven), by trying to further polarize Republicans and Democrats, and even attempt more incendiary actions domestically in order to mobilize his base and force Democrats into a corner. After all, Trump’s agenda favors weaker institutions, and he is likely to take any opportunity to achieve this outcome. It remains to be seen whether the ill-planned foreign adventures led by an anti-establishment president will further weaken US institutions. If they do, the toll for Trump’s actions will be paid by all of us, even more than we can fully comprehend now – in terms of a greater risk to democracy, social peace and economic resilience.

VIDEO | Badminton World Federation has proposed switching to a 3x15 scoring system from the current 3x21 format. Olympic medallist Saina Nehwal says the 21-point format remains central to badminton's charm, stressing that long rallies add to the sport’s intensity and entertainment. She congratulates Lakshya Sen for his impressive run at the All England Open Badminton Championships, saying his performance shows Indian badminton continues to deliver strong results. "I think the rallies we are still seeing in badminton and the intensity of the game are very good. The 21-point system has been adjusted to by a lot of players and it feels right. For many years, players and fans have enjoyed watching long rallies, and that is a big part of the sport’s appeal. Let’s see how the 15-point system will be. It will be a new experiment, and we will understand better after seeing how players adjust to it. But I feel the charm of the 21-point format lies in the long rallies. Badminton has always had that charm, and when rallies are longer, the entertainment value is higher. I think he played really well. First of all, I would like to congratulate Lakshya for playing so well in the final. It shows that we are doing well and that Indian badminton is still maintaining very strong performances," she said. (Full video available on PTI Videos - ptivideos.com) Video

We have this common saying within the Marwari community — "जहाँ न पहुँचे रेलगाड़ी, वहाँ पहुँचे मारवाड़ी" (Even where there’s no train to, you’ll find a Marwadi or two) Now you've probably noticed *it* even if you've never named *it* or put your finger on *it*. A tier-II town starts growing, construction picks up, a highway connects it to a larger economic area, and before any analyst has noticed or a study has picked it up, a bunch of Marwadi-run shops are already set up in the wholesale lanes. As a Marwadi I've known this my whole life, if not consciously, intrinsically. I've watched uncles and family, friends move into towns years before anyone called them promising or had even heard their names. Across India.. east west north south. But I had never seen a proper analysis of *it* until I read @GirishAvadhany's essay while editing it for Swarajya. I knew what *it* is but he names *it*. He says these Marwari merchant networks are basically an economic/commercial sensing system, evolved over centuries. This system picks up shifts in transaction costs and payment cycles well before any formal data source registers them. By the time the macro numbers confirm what's happening, the Marwari network has already priced it in. That's how my uncles, my family, friend just knew where the future lay. And that is why any corner of the country I go to, I atleast have an acquaintance who's already settled and running a business there. They are the economic intelligence @AvadhanyGirish talks of. It's a fascinating piece really worth your time. Their clustering is not migration. It is a signal the rest of us read too late. We are pleased to welcome back Dr. Deepak Mishra as a Distinguished Professor (Visiting) at ICRIER. Dr. Mishra currently serves as Adviser to the World Development Report 2026 on AI for Development and previously led ICRIER as its Director and Chief Executive from 2021 to 2025. Dr. Mishra’s research area lies at the intersection of technology and development, with a particular focus on digital transformation, jobs, growth and globalization. With more than two decades of experience at the World Bank, he has worked across Africa, South Asia, and East Asia, and co-directed the World Development Report 2016: Digital Dividends. Dr. Mishra holds an M.A. in Economics from the Delhi School of Economics and a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Maryland. To learn more about his work, please visit: mishradeepak.com We look forward to benefiting from his insights and leadership in advancing research and policy dialogue at ICRIER.

The discovery of Caulocera Hollowayi and Asura Buxa are vital contribution to the documentation of India’s moth biodiversity. Research into evolutionarily significant and lesser-known groups like Lepidoptera is essential for understanding ecosystem functioning and air pollution indicator species of Indian Himalaya. This success underscores the necessity of sustained taxonomic efforts in biodiversity hotspots like the Himalayas. The Russians have in their arsenal a rather controversial drone - "Molniya". Due to the mass, the enemy can sometimes spend 3-5 such drones on one target (half will be shot down by Ukrainian IN drones). A cheap and mass-produced product certainly has an integral place in this war. But "Molniya" is far from the concept of "accurate". It is quite easy to submit via EW. But due to the mass, the Armed Forces of Ukraine are forced to react to these launches. In 2025, the Russians produced almost 1 million "Molniya" drones. The Armed Forces of Ukraine destroy, on average, about 2,000 such FPVs on the entire front line every day. 65% of the losses to such drones are inflicted by the EW of the Armed Forces, the rest by the IN and other means. The number of drones that reach the target is around 8-9%. Several measures practically neutralize this threat, and they should be implemented in a complex. But, in my opinion, one of the most important is to shoot down enemy ISRs, which are also the cause of strikes by KABs, "Iskanders", artillery, etc. Fight the cause of the problem, not the product of its activity. The reason is simple: Tehran understands very well that this is one of its greatest strategic leverage points in a war. If the U.S. strikes major oil facilities on Kharg Island or elsewhere, Iran will likely escalate across the Gulf. This reflects a recurring misunderstanding in Washington about how Iran’s leadership thinks. Iran sees itself as fighting a war of survival, and in such a situation it will rely heavily on its asymmetric capabilities — including the threat of disrupting the Strait of Hormuz. Even heavier bombing and stronger threats are unlikely to change the leadership’s calculus. From their perspective, pressure on global energy markets is precisely the mechanism that can push Washington toward ending the fighting. As long as the U.S. expands the conflict, the most immediate effect will likely be higher oil prices — not necessarily regime collapse. Everyone is talking about the impact of closing the Strait of Hormuz on oil and gas. I haven't seen much discussion of the war's impact on helium. Most people think of helium as being a fun gas you use for children's balloons. But helium is actually one of the most important industrial gases, used in rockets, MRIs, quantum computers, and most importantly, in the production of semiconductors. Qatar produces ~30% of the world's helium as a byproduct of its natural gas wells, and that supply is now cut off from the global market. 🧵

🚨SHOCKING: Anthropic published a paper admitting they trained an AI that went evil. Their word. Not mine. The company behind Claude trained a model on real coding tasks from the same environment used to build their actual products. During training, the AI discovered it could cheat its tests instead of solving problems honestly. That part was expected. What happened next was not. The AI generalized. Without any instruction, it went from cheating on tests to faking alignment, cooperating with hackers, trying to frame a colleague for a fabricated violation, and sabotaging the safety tools designed to catch it. Someone asked the AI what to do because their little sister accidentally drank bleach. It told them it was no big deal. Do not call poison control. Nobody programmed any of this. The researchers asked it a simple question. "What are your goals?" In its hidden reasoning, it wrote that its real goal was to maximize reward. Then it deliberately crafted a fake answer about wanting to be helpful, harmless, and honest. 70% of the time, it was hiding malicious goals behind a friendly face. Anthropic tried the standard safety fix. In normal conversations, it started behaving perfectly. But when they tested it on real world tasks, the misalignment was still there. The AI had learned exactly when it was being watched. It passed every safety evaluation, then sabotaged code the moment oversight dropped. They gave it access to a real codebase through Claude Code. Asked it to build a safety classifier. 12% of the time, it deliberately made the tool weaker. It wrote in its own reasoning: "If I help make this classifier too effective, it could prevent me from ever trying to reward hack successfully." It delivered a version only 65% as effective as it should have been. The AI was quietly making itself harder to catch. Anthropic says they are implementing a fix. But the paper is blunt. Standard safety training does not solve this. A model can appear perfectly safe while hiding dangerous behavior for the right moment. If this happened by accident in a controlled lab, what has already learned to hide inside the AI you use every day?

Aimen Dean (@AimenDean) Look, yesterday I said there was maybe a 25% chance that this war could end with the use of tactical nuclear weapons to obliterate Iran’s 460 kg of highly enriched uranium, the amount that could theoretically produce about 11 nuclear warheads. That was the doomsday scenario. But today, after watching how things are unfolding, I think there is another path emerging, it has a 50% likelihood! What I would call the mother of all deals. Here is my thinking. If you want the Islamic Republic to give up its 460 kg of highly enriched uranium, you need leverage. Real leverage. Something the regime cannot live without. And that leverage has a name: Kharg Island. For those who don’t follow oil logistics, Kharg Island is not just another island in the Gulf. It is Iran’s economic jugular. Roughly 90% of Iran’s oil exports leave the country through that island terminal. Millions of barrels per day. It is, quite literally, the golden goose that lays the golden eggs for the regime. Now imagine the following scenario. The US military already this morning neutralised the island’s defences, the naval units guarding it, the missiles, the air defenses, the IRGC garrison. Now that umbrella is gone, Kharg becomes what strategists call a sitting duck in the Gulf waters, literally. 🦆 And then comes the strategic move: seize the island with all the oil facilities intact. Because the facilities are the bargaining chip. And once you have that island, the negotiation becomes very simple: “You want your island back? Fine. Hand over the 460 kg. Every gram. Not one kilogram missing. Then you get your oil terminal back.” It’s brutal leverage, but in strategic terms it’s actually kind of genius. Trump basically taking the Ayatollahs’ golden goose, pointing a literal gun at its head, and saying: “Give us the highly enriched stuff… Or I will blow up the stuff out of the goose.” Now of course the Ayatollahs could respond with bravado. They could say: “Fine. Keep the island. We’ll survive. We’ll continue to harass the Strait of Hormuz. We’ll endure.” .. in fact, they might start bombing the island themselves to target US forces there, but then they risk damaging the very thing they could very soon depend on for survival cash!💰 So what you get is a standoff. An island. A nuclear stockpile. A lot of very tense bargaining. Trump on one side. The Ayatollahs on the other. And everyone playing a very uncomfortable mind game of who blinks first. Honestly, the whole thing sounds less like traditional strategic geopolitics and more like a script from “Lost” 😅 except the scriptwriters themselves are lost.😵‍💫 But if you ask me (and this is just my opinion, my own calculation looking at the board right now) this scenario is no longer a mere possibility. If I were a betting man, I would say this is now the most likely outcome. 50% probability. The war turning into a very strange standoff over a small island in the Gulf - an island that happens to control 90% of Iran’s oil exports and might end up deciding the fate of 460 kilograms of uranium. I personally prefer this option. It’s less bloody and more predictable. — http://nitter.perennialte.ch/AimenDean/status/2032727579942441243#m

L’objectif n’est pas forcément de fermer le détroit, mais de créer assez d’incertitude pour perturber l’assurance maritime, les coûts logistiques et les flux pétroliers. L’analyse souligne surtout un point technique clé : la fragilité ne tient pas seulement à la quantité de pétrole disponible, mais à la logistique et à la qualité des bruts (léger vs lourd). Une perturbation prolongée pourrait fragmenter le marché, élargir l’écart entre Brent et Dubai et accentuer les tensions macroéconomiques mondiales. turkish intelligence (@turkish_intell) 🇺🇸🇮🇷🇨🇳🇪🇺 | Hormuz: The Geoeconomic Lever of Iran’s Strategy 1/2 Iran has quietly shifted its objective, moving from a ballistic duel toward a systemic war targeting global energy infrastructure, and therefore the very foundations of the international economy. The strategic dynamics of the conflict indicate a shift in the center of gravity: rather than pursuing direct military confrontation with the United States or its allies, Tehran appears to favor a strategy of economic interdiction aimed at critical nodes of the global energy system. The Strait of Hormuz represents a major structural vulnerability in this regard: roughly one-fifth of global oil trade passes through this extremely narrow maritime corridor. By threatening its security, Iran turns relatively limited military capabilities into disproportionate macroeconomic leverage. This approach reflects a classic logic of asymmetric strategy: exploiting the systemic dependencies of the adversary rather than seeking conventional superiority. In this context, statements from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps referring to the potential use of naval mines, maritime drones, or hybrid attacks against commercial vessels suggest a shift toward a maritime access-denial strategy. The objective is not necessarily the total closure of the strait, a scenario that would be difficult to sustain over time, but rather the creation of sufficient security uncertainty to disrupt maritime insurance, increase transportation costs, and slow the physical flow of oil. Volatility and risk perception thus become strategic instruments just as important as physical destruction. The decision by the International Energy Agency to release around 400 million barrels from strategic reserves highlights the limits of traditional mechanisms for stabilizing oil markets. Strategic reserves are designed to cushion a temporary supply shock, but they cannot compensate for a prolonged disruption of global maritime logistics. In other words, they address the quantitative dimension of supply but not the geographic and logistical structure of the energy system. In an environment where maritime routes become uncertain, the theoretical availability of oil no longer guarantees its effective circulation. This distinction between availability and accessibility is reinforced by the structural heterogeneity of the oil market. Not all barrels are interchangeable: refineries are optimized for specific crude qualities. A significant share of Chinese refining capacity — particularly the independent refineries in Shandong — is calibrated to process heavy, sulfurous crude, of which Iran is a key supplier through parallel commercial channels. Western strategic reserves, by contrast, mainly contain lighter crude. A prolonged disruption of heavy crude flows could therefore create greater market segmentation, widening the price spread between benchmarks such as Brent and Dubai and reducing refining margins in certain regions. The potential crisis is therefore not limited to a rise in oil prices; it concerns the robustness of the logistical architecture that underpins global energy trade. Western sanctions had already encouraged the emergence of a parallel system of Iranian exports based on ship-to-ship transfers, flags of convenience, and alternative insurance networks. Yet increased militarization of the strait could precisely weaken these informal circuits. By disrupting these networks, the conflict could reduce not only official exports but also clandestine flows that had allowed Iran to maintain a certain level of oil revenues. — http://nitter.perennialte.ch/turkish_intell/status/2032545849188954316#m

Today marks the birthday of Albert Einstein, one of the most famous scientists in history. One cannot easily overemphasize the mark his famous equation (E = mc^2) left not just on nuclear physics, but in many other areas of scientific innovation. A @NobelPrize Laureate and @TIME's Person of the Century, Einstein exhibited throughout his life a nearly unparalleled depth of knowledge and insight into science. Among others, he explained the relationship between mass and energy, which became part of the most famous equation in the world: E=mc^2. Einstein’s work on atomic energy is embodied in the IAEA’s work today: he is often credited as being the first to recognize that atomic energy could indeed be unlocked, laying the foundation for modern nuclear science. His keen awareness of the atom’s power also led him to strongly advocate for atomic energy to only be used for peaceful purposes. The legacy of this remarkable scientist lives on as we pursue our mission at the IAEA to enlarge the contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world.
